question: You have a web access log where each line starts with the client IP followed by other fields. Write a one-liner that prints the top 5 IP addresses by request count.
thoughtProcess: This is the canonical filter-extract-count-rank log task, so the interviewer wants to see fluency composing standard Unix tools into a pipeline. I restate the shape: the IP is the first whitespace-separated field, so awk '{print $1}' extracts it. To count occurrences I must group identical IPs together, which means sort first (because uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates), then uniq -c to attach counts. Finally I sort numerically in descending order by the count with sort -rn and take the first five lines with head. I would note the whole thing streams line by line so it handles very large logs with flat memory, and that if the IP were a different field I would just change the awk field number.

solution.code: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5

lineByLine: awk '{print $1}' access.log extracts the first field (the client IP) from every line. sort brings identical IPs next to each other, which is required because the next tool only collapses adjacent duplicates. uniq -c collapses each run of identical lines into one line prefixed with its count. sort -rn then sorts those count-prefixed lines numerically (-n) in reverse (-r) order, so the highest counts come first. head -n 5 keeps only the top five lines, giving the five busiest IPs.
timeComplexity: Dominated by the sort, so O(N log N) in the number of lines N; the awk, uniq, and head stages are linear. The pipeline streams, so it processes files larger than memory, with sort spilling to disk as needed.
spaceComplexity: O(U) for the distinct IPs held during counting where U is the number of unique IPs; sort may buffer and spill to disk for large inputs, keeping peak memory bounded.

alternativeApproaches.title: Count directly in awk with an associative array
alternativeApproaches.explanation: awk can tally counts in memory using an associative array keyed by IP, avoiding the first sort entirely, then you sort only the aggregated results. This is faster on huge logs with relatively few distinct IPs because it collapses the data before sorting.
alternativeApproaches.code: awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (ip in c) print c[ip], ip}' access.log | sort -rn | head -n 5

alternativeApproaches.title: Filter to a subset first
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If you only want the top IPs among error responses or a time window, add a grep or an awk condition before counting so the expensive stages process far less data, for example grep ' 500 ' access.log before the extraction.

followUps.question: Why must you sort before uniq?
followUps.answer: uniq only detects and collapses duplicate lines that are adjacent to each other; it does not scan the whole input for all copies of a value. So identical IPs scattered throughout the file would be counted as separate single occurrences unless you first sort to bring all copies of each IP together. Sorting groups them, and then uniq -c can correctly count each group. Forgetting the sort is a classic bug that produces wildly wrong counts, which is why sort immediately precedes uniq in this idiom.

followUps.question: How would the awk associative array version scale differently?
followUps.answer: The awk array approach aggregates counts in a single streaming pass, holding one entry per distinct IP in memory, then sorts only the aggregated results. This avoids sorting the entire raw log, so when there are many lines but relatively few unique IPs it is substantially faster and reads the data once. Its limit is memory: it must hold all distinct keys at once, so if the number of unique IPs is enormous it could use a lot of memory, whereas the sort-based pipeline spills to disk and handles unbounded cardinality at the cost of the full sort.

question: Write a command to find and remove duplicate lines from a large text file, preserving a single copy of each unique line. Then describe how to do it without changing line order.
thoughtProcess: Deduplication is a common file-cleaning task. The simplest approach uses sort -u, which sorts and outputs unique lines in one step, or sort | uniq. But the interviewer will probe the tradeoff: sorting changes the original line order. If order must be preserved, sort is the wrong tool, and the idiomatic answer is an awk one-liner that keeps a set of seen lines and prints each line only the first time it appears. I would present both, explaining that sort-based dedup is memory-efficient because sort spills to disk, while the awk approach preserves order but must hold all unique lines in memory. I would also mention writing to a temp file and moving it, rather than editing in place, to stay safe.

solution.code:
# Dedup (order not preserved) - simplest and memory-friendly
sort -u input.txt > output.txt

# Dedup preserving original order
awk '!seen[$0]++' input.txt > output.txt

lineByLine: sort -u input.txt sorts all lines and emits only unique ones, collapsing duplicates, writing the result to output.txt; this reorders the lines. In the order-preserving version, awk '!seen[$0]++' uses the whole line ($0) as a key into the associative array seen. The expression seen[$0]++ returns the current count (0 the first time) and then increments it; the leading ! makes the condition true only when the count was 0, so awk's default action prints the line the first time it is seen and never again, preserving the original order.
timeComplexity: sort -u is O(N log N) in the number of lines. The awk approach is O(N) time, a single linear pass, since each line is a constant-time hash lookup and insert.
spaceComplexity: sort -u keeps memory bounded by buffering and spilling to disk, so it handles very large files. The awk approach is O(U) memory for the U unique lines it must remember, which can be large if there are many distinct lines.

alternativeApproaches.title: sort then uniq explicitly
alternativeApproaches.explanation: sort input.txt | uniq is equivalent to sort -u and makes the two steps explicit; uniq -d would instead show only the duplicated lines, and uniq -u only lines that appear exactly once, which is useful for auditing duplicates.

alternativeApproaches.title: In-place safe replacement
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Never redirect back into the same file you are reading, as that truncates it before reading. Write to a temporary file and move it atomically: awk '!seen[$0]++' input.txt > tmp && mv tmp input.txt, so a failure leaves the original intact.

followUps.question: How does awk '!seen[$0]++' preserve order while sort does not?
followUps.answer: The awk approach walks the file in its original order and prints each line the moment it first appears, remembering which lines it has already emitted in the seen array, so the output keeps the sequence of first appearances exactly as in the input. sort, by contrast, must reorder the entire file to group duplicates together before removing them, so its output is sorted, not in original order. The tradeoff is that awk must hold every unique line in memory to remember it, whereas sort can spill to disk and thus handle inputs with more unique data than fits in RAM.

followUps.question: Why should you avoid redirecting output back to the input file?
followUps.answer: When you write cmd input.txt > input.txt, the shell opens and truncates input.txt for writing before the command starts reading it, so the input is wiped out and you get an empty or corrupt result. To edit a file safely you write to a separate temporary file and then move it over the original with mv, which is atomic within a filesystem, or use a tool's dedicated in-place option that handles this correctly. This staging-then-move pattern also means a failure mid-operation leaves the original file untouched rather than destroyed.

question: Write a command to find which directories are consuming the most disk space under /var, showing the top 10 largest.
thoughtProcess: This is a disk-usage triage task, exactly what you do when a server is filling up. The right tool is du, which reports disk usage per directory. I want a summary per subdirectory, not every file, so I use du with a depth limit or run it on the immediate children. Then I sort by size descending and take the top ten. The subtlety is human-readable versus sortable sizes: du -h gives friendly units like G and M but they do not sort numerically, so I either sort by raw bytes then format, or use sort -h which understands human-readable suffixes. I would also mention running with sudo if some directories are not readable, and redirecting permission errors so they do not clutter output.
lineByLine: du -h --max-depth=1 /var reports the total disk usage of /var and each of its immediate subdirectories in human-readable units (-h), with --max-depth=1 preventing it from listing every nested file. 2>/dev/null discards permission-denied error messages so the output stays clean. sort -rh sorts the results in reverse (-r) using human-readable numeric comparison (-h), which correctly understands suffixes like K, M, and G, so the largest directories come first. head -n 10 keeps the top ten space consumers.
timeComplexity: O(F) in the number of files and directories under /var, since du must traverse the tree to sum sizes; the sort of the small per-directory summary is negligible.
spaceComplexity: O(D) where D is the number of immediate subdirectories being summarized and sorted, which is small; du's traversal uses bounded memory.

alternativeApproaches.title: Sort by raw bytes for reliability
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If sort -h is unavailable, output raw byte counts and sort numerically, then optionally format. du -b or du without -h gives sortable numbers: du --max-depth=1 /var | sort -rn | head -n 10 sorts by size reliably across systems.

alternativeApproaches.title: Interactive exploration with ncdu
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For hunting down space interactively, ncdu (if installed) presents a navigable, sorted view of disk usage you can drill into, which is faster than repeated du commands when you do not yet know where the space is going.

followUps.question: Why can du -h output be misleading when sorted with a plain sort?
followUps.answer: The -h flag prints sizes with unit suffixes like 500K, 2M, and 1G, but a plain lexical or numeric sort does not understand those suffixes, so it would sort 900K after 2G because it compares the leading numbers or the raw strings rather than the true magnitudes. You must either use sort -h, which is aware of human-readable suffixes and orders them by actual size, or sort by raw byte counts (du without -h) and format afterward. Otherwise the ranking is wrong precisely when it matters, mixing up gigabytes and kilobytes.

followUps.question: What is the difference between du and df, and when do you use each?
followUps.answer: df reports usage at the filesystem level, how full each mounted filesystem is overall, which answers whether and where you are out of space. du reports usage per directory or file, which answers what is consuming the space within a filesystem. In a disk-full incident you typically start with df -h to confirm which filesystem is full, then use du on that filesystem to drill down and find the offending directories. They are complementary: df for the big picture, du for pinpointing the culprits.

question: Write a Python script that reads configuration from environment variables with sensible defaults and required-value validation, suitable for a data pipeline.
thoughtProcess: This tests whether the candidate follows the twelve-factor practice of configuring apps via the environment rather than hardcoding. I want to read settings from os.environ, provide defaults for optional values, coerce types (env vars are always strings), and fail fast with a clear error if a required value like a database URL is missing. I would centralize this in one config module so the rest of the code imports typed settings rather than scattering os.environ calls everywhere. I would also avoid printing secrets. The key design points are: required vs optional, type coercion, and failing loudly at startup with an actionable message instead of crashing deep in the pipeline later.
lineByLine: ConfigError is a custom exception so configuration problems are distinguishable and clear. get_required reads an environment variable and raises immediately if it is missing or empty, enforcing that critical settings are present. get_int reads an optional variable, returns the provided default when absent, and coerces the string to an integer, raising a helpful error if the value is not a valid integer, since environment variables are always strings. The Config class assembles all settings in one place: database_url is required, while batch_size, environment, and retries have defaults. Constructing config at module import means the program fails fast at startup with an actionable message rather than crashing later mid-run.
timeComplexity: O(1); reading a handful of environment variables and coercing them is constant work done once at startup.
spaceComplexity: O(1); the configuration object holds a fixed, small number of values.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use a settings library
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Libraries like pydantic-settings (or environs) declare a typed settings model that reads from the environment, validates types, applies defaults, and produces clear errors automatically, reducing boilerplate and giving type safety for larger configs.
alternativeApproaches.code:
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str
    batch_size: int = 1000
    environment: str = "dev"

settings = Settings()

alternativeApproaches.title: Layered config with .env for local dev
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Load a git-ignored .env file for local development (for example with python-dotenv) so developers get convenient local values, while real environments inject variables through the deployment system. The code still reads from the environment, keeping one code path across environments.

followUps.question: Why should configuration fail fast at startup rather than when a value is first used?
followUps.answer: Failing fast means the program checks all required configuration the moment it starts, so a missing or invalid setting surfaces immediately with a clear error before any real work begins. If instead you only discover a missing database URL deep inside the pipeline after processing has started, you may have done partial work, written incomplete data, or wasted a long run, and the error appears far from its true cause. Validating configuration at startup gives an actionable message right away and prevents the pipeline from proceeding in a misconfigured, unsafe state.

followUps.question: Why must you coerce and validate types when reading environment variables?
followUps.answer: Environment variables are always strings, so a numeric setting like batch size arrives as text like '1000' and must be converted to an int before use, or arithmetic and comparisons will misbehave. Validating the conversion, and raising a clear error if the value is not a valid integer, catches typos and misconfiguration at startup rather than letting a bad value cause a confusing failure later. Explicit type coercion with validation turns silent, hard-to-trace bugs into loud, self-explaining configuration errors, which is exactly what you want for reliable pipelines.

question: Write a robust bash script that downloads a file, verifies it is non-empty, and loads it, exiting with the correct status and cleaning up on failure.
thoughtProcess: This tests production-grade shell scripting, not just the happy path. I want strict mode at the top so any failure aborts and no unset variable slips through. I use a temporary file created safely with mktemp, and register a trap so it is cleaned up whether the script succeeds or fails. I download to the temp file, check the download's exit status, and verify the file is actually non-empty before proceeding, because a successful HTTP call can still yield an empty or error body. Only if everything passes do I load the data. I make sure the script exits non-zero on any failure so a scheduler sees it. The emphasis is failing loudly, cleaning up, and returning honest exit codes.

solution.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

URL="https://example.com/data.csv"
tmpfile="$(mktemp)"

# Clean up the temp file on any exit, success or failure
trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"' EXIT

echo "Downloading $URL"
if ! curl -fsS "$URL" -o "$tmpfile"; then
    echo "ERROR: download failed" >&2
    exit 1
fi

if [ ! -s "$tmpfile" ]; then
    echo "ERROR: downloaded file is empty" >&2
    exit 2
fi

echo "Loading data"
if ! ./load_data.sh "$tmpfile"; then
    echo "ERROR: load step failed" >&2
    exit 3
fi

echo "Done"
exit 0

lineByLine: set -euo pipefail turns on strict mode: exit on any error (-e), error on unset variables (-u), and fail a pipeline if any stage fails (pipefail). mktemp creates a unique temporary file safely. trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"' EXIT registers cleanup that runs whenever the script exits, so the temp file never lingers even on failure. curl -fsS downloads with -f making HTTP errors return a failure code, -sS staying quiet but still showing real errors; if it fails the script logs to stderr and exits 1. The -s test checks the file is non-empty, exiting 2 if not, since a request can succeed yet return nothing. The load step is checked and exits 3 on failure. Each stage returns a distinct non-zero code, and a clean run exits 0.
timeComplexity: Dominated by the download and load steps themselves, which depend on file size and network and the load logic; the script's own control flow is O(1).
spaceComplexity: O(S) disk for the temporary file of size S; the script holds no data in memory itself.

alternativeApproaches.title: Atomic move into place
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Instead of loading directly from the temp file, download to a temp path and atomically move it to a stable destination only after verification, so downstream consumers never see a partial file: mv "$tmpfile" "$final" after the non-empty check.

alternativeApproaches.title: Add retries with backoff
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For transient network failures, wrap the download in a retry loop with exponential backoff so brief blips self-heal, only failing after a capped number of attempts, which improves reliability against flaky sources without masking persistent failures.

followUps.question: Why check that the downloaded file is non-empty even after a successful curl?
followUps.answer: A download can complete successfully at the transport level yet return an empty body or an error page, for example if the server responded with an error, an empty result, or a truncated response that still counted as a completed transfer. If the script proceeded to load an empty file it would silently load nothing while reporting success, corrupting the pipeline. Checking with the -s test that the file actually has content, and using curl -f so HTTP error statuses become failures, guards against these cases so the script only proceeds when it genuinely has data.

followUps.question: What role does the trap play, and why use distinct exit codes?
followUps.answer: The trap on EXIT guarantees the temporary file is removed no matter how the script ends, success, error, or an exit triggered by strict mode, so it never leaves stray files that could fill disk or confuse later runs. Distinct exit codes for each failure stage (download, empty file, load) make failures self-identifying: a scheduler or an operator reading the exit code immediately knows which step failed without parsing logs. Together they make the script both clean and observable, cleaning up after itself while returning honest, specific status that automation can act on.

question: You committed a large data file and a secret to Git across several commits, then pushed. Describe the exact commands and steps to fully clean this up.
thoughtProcess: This is a Git history-surgery scenario that also tests security judgment. The critical first point, which separates senior from junior answers, is that pushing a secret means it is compromised, so the very first action is to rotate the credential, not to clean history. Only then do I address the repository. Because the file and secret exist across multiple commits and were pushed, a simple new commit removing them is insufficient; they remain in history and the repo stays bloated. I must rewrite history across all commits with a purpose-built tool like git filter-repo (the modern recommendation) or BFG, force-push the rewritten history, and have all collaborators re-clone. Finally I add prevention: gitignore, secret scanning, and moving the file out of Git. I will lay out the ordered steps precisely.

solution.code:
# STEP 0 (do this FIRST): rotate the leaked secret at its source.
# The moment it was pushed, treat it as compromised. Rewriting history
# does NOT undo the exposure.

# STEP 1: remove the large file and the secret from ALL history
# Using git filter-repo (recommended over the deprecated filter-branch)
git filter-repo --path data/big_file.csv --invert-paths
git filter-repo --path config/secrets.env --invert-paths

# STEP 2: force-push the rewritten history to the remote
git push origin --force --all
git push origin --force --tags

# STEP 3: have every collaborator re-clone (their old clones still
# contain the removed objects and would reintroduce them).

# STEP 4: prevent recurrence
echo 'data/big_file.csv' >> .gitignore
echo 'config/secrets.env' >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore && git commit -m 'Ignore data files and secrets'

lineByLine: Step 0 rotates the secret first, because once pushed it must be assumed compromised and no history edit can un-expose it. Step 1 uses git filter-repo with --path and --invert-paths to remove the specified paths from every commit in history, so the large file and the secrets file no longer exist anywhere in the rewritten history. Step 2 force-pushes all branches and tags, replacing the remote's history with the cleaned version. Step 3 requires collaborators to re-clone, because their existing clones still hold the old objects and a normal pull would reintroduce them or cause divergence. Step 4 adds the paths to .gitignore and commits it, so the same files cannot be accidentally committed again.
timeComplexity: The history rewrite is proportional to the size of the repository history, O(total objects across all commits), since filter-repo processes every commit; force-push transfers the rewritten history.
spaceComplexity: O(repo size) for the rewritten object store during the operation; afterward the repository is smaller because the large objects are gone.

alternativeApproaches.title: BFG Repo-Cleaner
alternativeApproaches.explanation: BFG is a faster, simpler tool for the common cases of deleting large files or replacing secret text across history. It is easier to invoke than filter-repo for straightforward removals, though filter-repo is more flexible and is the officially recommended successor to filter-branch.
alternativeApproaches.code:
bfg --delete-files big_file.csv
bfg --replace-text secrets.txt   # scrubs matching secret strings
git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now --aggressive

alternativeApproaches.title: Prevent with hooks and scanning
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add a pre-commit hook or a secret-scanning tool that blocks commits containing secrets or oversized files before they ever land, and enable server-side secret scanning on the host, so this class of mistake is caught at commit time rather than requiring painful history surgery afterward.

followUps.question: Why is rotating the secret more urgent than cleaning the history?
followUps.answer: Once a secret is pushed to a remote, you must assume it has already been seen or copied, by scanners, other clones, logs, or attackers, so it is effectively public regardless of what you do to the repository afterward. Rewriting history removes it from the codebase but cannot retract copies that already exist elsewhere. The only way to truly neutralize the exposure is to invalidate the leaked credential by rotating it, so even if someone has it, it no longer works. That is why rotation comes first and history cleanup, while still necessary, is secondary.

followUps.question: Why isn't a normal commit deleting the file enough?
followUps.answer: A commit that deletes the file only removes it from the current tip going forward; every historical commit that contained the file still holds it, so the large file and the secret remain fully present and retrievable in the repository's history, and the repo stays bloated. Anyone can check out an older commit and recover them. To actually purge them you must rewrite every affected commit to remove the content, which is what filter-repo or BFG do. Because that rewrites history, it requires a force-push and re-clones, which is precisely why prevention is far preferable to remediation.

followUps.question: What must collaborators do after the history is rewritten, and why?
followUps.answer: They must re-clone the repository, or carefully reset their local copy to the rewritten remote history, because their existing clones still contain the old commits with the large file and secret. If they simply pull, their local history diverges from the rewritten remote and a merge could reintroduce exactly the objects you removed, undoing the cleanup. Coordinating so everyone discards the old history and adopts the cleaned version is essential; otherwise the removed content leaks back in. This disruption to the whole team is a major reason to prevent such commits with ignore files and scanning in the first place.
